Pregnancy

Slow labour progress: assessment, support and birth options

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A labour that feels long is not necessarily a labour that has stopped progressing. The maternity team looks at changes over time, your condition and how your baby is coping. Knowing which stage is being discussed can make an unexpected change of plan easier to understand. Seek help for concerning symptoms at any point rather than waiting for a particular number of hours.

Start by asking which stage is being measured

The cervix is the lower part of the womb, above the vagina. During the first stage it thins and opens; full dilation is about 10 cm. The second stage runs from full dilation until birth. Early, latent labour can last many hours or days, with contractions that do not yet form a regular pattern.

A duration quoted for one stage is not the length of the whole experience. NHS information describes about 8–18 hours from established labour to full dilation in a first pregnancy, often less in later pregnancies. These are descriptive ranges. They are not a deadline for everyone, and a first birth, a subsequent birth or twins cannot be assessed using one universal clock.

Slow progress and arrest mean different things

Slow progress means change is occurring more slowly than expected; arrest means progress has stopped under defined clinical conditions. In ACOG’s 2024 framework, active labour begins at 6 cm. Active-phase arrest requires no further dilation with broken waters despite four hours of adequate contractions, or six hours of inadequate contractions with oxytocin. These criteria must not be applied earlier.

For pushing, ACOG uses more than three hours in a first birth or two hours after a previous birth as prolonged, with individual assessment of descent, rotation and wellbeing. Earlier intervention can be necessary. NICE uses a different established-labour assessment pathway. Ask which framework applies locally. An induction that has not reached active labour is a separate assessment, not automatically active-phase arrest.

What the team checks when progress slows

The examination considers whether the cervix is changing, how the baby is moving down and turning, and whether contractions are effective. A baby’s position and the relationship between the baby and the pelvis may matter. These findings are assessed together; a size estimate or a painful contraction alone cannot explain the whole course of labour.

Staff also assess your temperature, pulse, blood pressure, comfort and the baby’s heart rate. Vaginal examinations should have an explanation and your consent. In selected cases, an internal pressure catheter can help measure contractions after the waters have broken when active labour is slow or external monitoring is inadequate. It is not a routine requirement for every lengthy labour.

Support continues while the plan is reviewed

Tell the team if you are exhausted, frightened or struggling with pain. Ask about rest, a more comfortable position, help from your birth companion and available pain relief. A long or difficult experience is not evidence that you have failed. Staff should explain what they are waiting to see and when they will reassess.

Follow the team’s advice about eating and drinking. Drinking when thirsty is different from forcing large amounts of water; excessive fluid can be harmful, particularly with intravenous fluids or oxytocin. Ask for help emptying your bladder if needed. Comfort measures can make care more manageable, but they are not substitutes for assessment of a suspected obstruction or an unwell baby.

Strengthening labour requires monitoring

If appropriate, clinicians may discuss breaking the waters or giving oxytocin through a vein to strengthen labour already underway. This is called augmentation. Ask what benefit is expected, what alternatives remain and how the response will be checked. Treatment should follow assessment of the reason for slow progress, rather than an assumption that stronger contractions are always better.

Oxytocin can produce excessive contractions, so the baby’s heart rate and contraction pattern need continuous monitoring. Staff may reduce or stop the infusion if a problem develops and reassess before restarting. Never adjust a pump or use medicines or herbal products to speed labour yourself. Consent and pain-relief needs remain part of the discussion as treatment changes.

How assisted birth or caesarean may enter the plan

Once the cervix is fully open, forceps or vacuum assistance may help when pushing is not bringing the baby down, you are very tired or the baby needs to be born sooner. The baby’s head needs to have descended into the pelvis. Before recommending assistance, the clinician establishes its position and assesses estimated size and whether vaginal birth appears feasible. The procedure requires appropriate expertise and suitable clinical conditions.

Assisted vaginal birth can avoid surgery, but carries risks including injury to the vaginal or perineal tissues and, less commonly, the baby. It may not succeed. Caesarean birth may be the safer option when assistance is unsuitable or unsuccessful, when active-phase arrest is confirmed, or when another urgent concern requires it. Ask the team to explain the recommendation, alternatives and urgency in your situation.

Risks are assessed, not assumed from elapsed time

A prolonged or arrested labour can be associated with infection, heavy bleeding after birth and concerns about the baby. These outcomes are not inevitable, and the duration alone does not establish their cause. Preparation for bleeding matters because the course of labour is one of several risk factors. Most people with bleeding risk factors still do not have a postpartum haemorrhage.

Continuous monitoring may be advised for confirmed delay or other risk factors. A heart-rate trace is interpreted alongside the whole situation; a change does not by itself prove injury. Meconium, the baby’s first stool, can colour the waters and prompt additional assessment. It may signal concern, but its appearance alone cannot tell you how the baby is coping or dictate the route of birth.

Symptoms and your recovery deserve attention

Contact maternity care urgently for waters breaking, bleeding, reduced baby movements or possible labour before 37 weeks. A fever of 38°C or higher, severe persistent abdominal pain, fainting, chest pain or breathing difficulty needs immediate medical attention. In hospital, alert staff straight away. Call emergency services for collapse, severe breathing difficulty or apparently imminent birth with a strong urge to push.

After birth, report increasing or heavy bleeding, fever, feeling unwell or bleeding accompanied by dizziness immediately. Ask what happened during labour and what follow-up you or your baby need. If distressing memories, anxiety or sleep difficulties persist, request support. A review of the experience can help explain decisions and prepare for future care without promising that another labour will follow the same course.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Labour frameworks differ between services; clinical thresholds are not instructions to wait at home.

The maternity team must assess progress, wellbeing and suitable options in real time.

Public information supports discussion and cannot diagnose arrest or select a procedure.

How BeMama can help

BeMama helps explain labour terminology and prepare questions. It cannot assess cervical change, interpret fetal monitoring or decide when your baby should be born.

When to seek help

Seek urgent maternity advice for leaking waters, bleeding, reduced movement or possible labour before 37 weeks. Fever, severe persistent pain, fainting, chest pain or breathing difficulty needs immediate care. Use emergency services for collapse, severe breathing difficulty or imminent birth with a strong urge to push. Do not alter labour medicines yourself.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The stage of labour matters more than a single total-hour label.
  • Slow progress and confirmed arrest require different clinical assessments.
  • Monitoring considers both your condition and the baby’s response.
  • Augmentation, assisted birth and caesarean each need an individual discussion.
  • Concerning symptoms need attention immediately, whatever the clock says.

Frequently asked questions

How long should vaginal labour take?

There is wide variation, especially in the early stage. Ask what stage a quoted time refers to and how your own progress will be reviewed. A previous birth or a multiple pregnancy does not create one reliable total-hour deadline.

What does prolonged labour mean?

It describes a longer-than-expected course, but clinicians need to specify the stage and findings. Slow change is different from stopped progress. Diagnosis and treatment cannot be chosen from elapsed time alone.

Why might labour progress slowly?

Contractions, cervical change and the baby’s movement through the pelvis all matter. Position and the wider clinical circumstances can contribute. Assessment looks for the reason rather than assuming you need stronger contractions or have done something wrong.

What complications are possible?

Infection, heavy bleeding after birth and concerns about the baby can occur, but are not inevitable. Monitoring and reassessment help the team decide when continuing labour remains appropriate and when birth should be expedited.

Does slow labour always mean a caesarean?

No. The options depend on the findings and response to care. Clinicians may recommend assisted vaginal birth in suitable circumstances. Confirmed arrest or an urgent problem can make caesarean birth appropriate.

What should I ask when the plan changes?

Ask what has changed, how you and the baby are doing, what the options are and when another review will happen. Tell the team about pain, exhaustion and your preferences. Urgent symptoms should be reported immediately rather than saved for the next planned check.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
